title: A/B Test Structure and Lift
summary: Introduces the structure of a randomised A/B test (control group, treatment group, metric) and the concept of lift (relative improvement) using QuickRide's checkout-button experiment. Learners identify the parts of an experiment and compute lift from control and treatment conversion rates.

steps.title: Two groups, one metric, one baseline
steps.lede: QuickRide's product team wants to know whether a redesigned checkout button gets more users to complete an order. Rather than guess, they run a controlled test — showing each user one version at random and measuring what happens.

blocks.text: Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called **experiments**. When the assignment includes randomisation, it is called a **randomised experiment**. Researchers randomly assign cases to a **control group** and a **treatment group** so that differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled are evened out.

**A/B testing** works by showing two variants of a page or experience to users at random: the original (**control, or A**) and a modified version (**variation, or B**). Engagement with each version is measured and then compared against the baseline — the control. For the checkout button: the existing button is A, the redesigned button is B, and the metric compared is the share of each group that completes an order.

segments.label: Defining A/B test structure: control group, treatment group, and the metric tracked
segments.summary: A/B testing (also called split testing) grew out of randomized controlled trials. The core idea: show the new or varied version of a product to one sample of users — the experimental group — and the existing version to a separate sample — the control group. The difference in product performance between the two groups is then tracked over the test period. If the varied version underperforms, the business can decide whether to refine it or explore other directions.

steps.title: Randomised vs non-randomised
steps.lede: Test your understanding of what makes an experiment randomised.

public.prompt: QuickRide's product team wants to test whether a redesigned checkout button increases order completion. They randomly assign each app user to see either the original button (control) or the redesigned button (treatment), then measure the share of each group that completes an order. Is this a randomised experiment?

options.text: Yes — users are randomly assigned to control or treatment, so differences between the groups are evened out.
No — users choose which button they see, so the two groups may differ in ways that affect the outcome.
No — the team assigns users by convenience (e.g., time of day), not by random assignment.
No — this is an observational study because the team is observing user behavior, not assigning treatments.

opt_yes.message: Correct. Random assignment evens out differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled, making this a randomised experiment. Each user is randomly shown one version or the other.

opt_no_choice.message: Users do not choose which button they see. The product team randomly assigns each user to control or treatment. When researchers assign treatments and include randomisation, it is a randomised experiment.

opt_no_convenience.message: The team does not assign by convenience. Each user is randomly shown one version or the other. Random assignment is what makes this a randomised experiment.

opt_no_observational.message: This is not an observational study. The team is assigning treatments (which button each user sees), not just observing. Studies where researchers assign treatments are called experiments; when the assignment includes randomisation, it is a randomised experiment.

correct.message: Exactly right. Random assignment is the key feature that makes this a randomised experiment.

incorrect.message: Think about who decides which button each user sees. Is it the user, or is it the product team assigning users at random?

hints: The prompt says users are 'randomly assigned' to see one version or the other. Who is doing the assigning?
Studies where researchers assign treatments to cases are called experiments. When the assignment includes randomisation, it is a randomised experiment.

steps.title: Turning raw rates into a single comparison figure
steps.lede: The checkout test is done: the control button converted 20 % of users, the redesigned button converted 22 %. Those two numbers need to be turned into a comparison that's easy to talk about — that's where lift comes in.

blocks.text: **Relative improvement (lift)** is the percentage difference in the variation's conversion rate over the baseline (control) conversion rate. For example, a 10 % relative improvement over a 25 % baseline means the variation's conversion rate is 27.5 %. Relative improvement describes the variation's change **as a percentage of the baseline's rate** — not as a percentage-point difference.

Applying that to the checkout test: treatment rate 22 % minus control rate 20 % is a **2-percentage-point** absolute difference. As a percentage of the 20 % baseline: 2 ÷ 20 × 100 = **10 % lift**. The redesigned button produced a 10 % relative improvement over the original.

result_of.sql: SELECT "group", users, conversions, conversion_rate FROM ab_test_summary WHERE "group" = 'control'
SELECT "group", users, conversions, conversion_rate FROM ab_test_summary WHERE "group" = 'treatment'

blocks.takeaway: Absolute difference: 0.22 − 0.20 = 0.02 (2 pp). Lift: 0.02 ÷ 0.20 × 100 = 10 % — the redesigned button produced a 10 % relative improvement over the baseline.

blocks.text: Analyzing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a **positive**, **negative**, or **neutral** effect compared with the baseline (control). A **positive lift** means the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test. A **negative lift** means it came out below. A **neutral** result means the rates were effectively the same.

steps.title: Positive, negative, or neutral?
steps.lede: Practise classifying an A/B test outcome by its direction.

public.prompt: An A/B test compared two email subject lines. The control (A) had a 15% open rate; the variation (B) had a 12% open rate. How would you classify this test's outcome?

options.text: Negative — the variation's rate came out below the control's in this test.
Positive — the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test.
Neutral — the rates were effectively the same.
Inconclusive — you need to know the sample size before classifying the outcome.

opt_negative.message: Correct. The variation's 12% open rate is below the control's 15%, so this is a negative outcome. The variation underperformed the baseline in this test.

opt_positive.message: The variation's rate (12%) is below the control's rate (15%), not above. A positive outcome means the variation came out above the control.

opt_neutral.message: The rates are not the same: 12% vs 15% is a 3-percentage-point difference. A neutral outcome means the rates were effectively the same.

opt_inconclusive.message: Sample size matters for statistical significance, but the question asks how to classify the outcome based on the observed rates. The variation's 12% is below the control's 15%, so the outcome is negative.

correct.message: Exactly right. The variation's rate came out below the control's, so this is a negative outcome.

incorrect.message: Compare the two rates: control 15%, variation 12%. Which one is higher?

hints: A positive outcome means the variation's rate came out above the control's. A negative outcome means it came out below.

solution_files.content:
POSITIVE = "Positive"
NEGATIVE = "Negative"
NEUTRAL = "Neutral"
SUFFIX = " lift of "
PCT = "%"

def compute_lift(control_rate, treatment_rate):
    lift = treatment_rate / control_rate * 100.0 - 100.0
    direction = POSITIVE if lift > 0.0 else NEGATIVE if lift < 0.0 else NEUTRAL
    return f"{direction}{SUFFIX}{lift}{PCT}"

print(compute_lift(0.10, 0.12))
print(compute_lift(0.15, 0.12))
print(compute_lift(0.25, 0.25))

steps.title: What you've learned
steps.lede: Every A/B test has the same three parts, and lift turns the raw rates into one interpretable figure.

blocks.text: Every A/B test has a **control group**, a **treatment group**, and the **measure** being compared between them. The treatment group's result is compared against the control — the baseline. Analysing the results means determining whether the variation had a **positive, negative, or neutral** effect. **Lift** puts the observed difference into one figure: a positive lift means the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test; a negative lift means it came out below.

remediation_steps.title: What makes an experiment randomised?
remediation_steps.lede: The check asked you to distinguish a randomised experiment from a non-randomised study. Here's the key contrast.

blocks.text: Studies where researchers **assign** treatments to cases are called **experiments**. When that assignment includes **randomisation**, it is a **randomised experiment**. Randomly assigning cases to a control group and a treatment group evens out differences between the groups that cannot otherwise be controlled — that's what makes the comparison fair.

A non-randomised study lets participants choose their own group, or assigns them by convenience. Without random assignment, the two groups may differ in ways that affect the outcome — so you can't be sure the treatment caused any difference you observe. In the checkout-button test, users are randomly shown one version or the other, which is what makes it a randomised experiment.

blocks.text: Analysing an A/B test's results means determining whether the variation had a **positive**, **negative**, or **neutral** effect compared with the baseline (control). A **positive lift** means the variation's rate came out above the control's in this test. A **negative lift** means it came out below. A **neutral** result means the rates were effectively the same.

remediation_steps.title: Computing lift step by step
remediation_steps.lede: The hands-on asked you to compute lift. Here's the calculation laid out clearly.

blocks.text: **Lift formula:** (treatment rate − control rate) ÷ control rate × 100. For the checkout test: (0.22 − 0.20) ÷ 0.20 × 100 = **10 % lift**. This is a relative improvement — it expresses the variation's change as a percentage of the baseline's rate, not as a raw percentage-point difference.

Three cases to check your function against: (1) control=0.20, treatment=0.22 → **+10 % (positive)**. (2) control=0.25, treatment=0.20 → **−20 % (negative)**. (3) control=0.30, treatment=0.30 → **0 % (neutral)**. A positive lift means the variation's rate came out above the control's; a negative lift means it came out below.
